title: F Blues

original_tune.why: It is a 12-bar blues in the same key.

listen_explainer: This sheet is a 12-bar blues in concert F (your D), the most common blues key in jazz. Charlie Parker's "Now's the Time" is a blues in the same key, so these are recordings of it. Find them on YouTube, Spotify, Apple Music or any streaming service: search the artist's name plus "Now's the Time". Listen through once just for the feel, then play the Section 1 arpeggios along with the recording.

recordings.album: The Complete Savoy & Dial Master Takes
recordings.note: The original, and the most famous alto blues on record. Listen to how relaxed and bluesy Bird sounds, and how his lines land on chord tones.

recordings.album: Now's the Time: The Quartet of Charlie Parker
recordings.note: Bird again eight years later, with just a rhythm section. Compare it with the first version: faster, cleaner, same blues.
A clear, strong alto sound. Listen for how every phrase outlines the chord it is over, like your arpeggios.
A warm, blues-soaked alto. Notice how much she says with simple ideas and space.
Tenor sax, not alto. Hear how he plays with the rhythm of one small idea across the whole chorus.

licks_intro: A ii-V-I (two-five-one) is the most common chord move in jazz, and the blues has it in two places: bar 4 (into the IV chord) and the turnaround at the end. Each lick lands on the 3rd of the chord it resolves to. Orange notes are the lick. Licks 1 and 2 are short (one bar); Lick 3 is the long turnaround over bars 9 and 10.

lick_groups.title: Lick 1 · Step down
lick_groups.note: walk down the scale from the 3rd of the ii chord, then jump up through the V chord and fall onto the 3rd of the next chord. Use it in bar 4 (into the IV chord) and bar 12 (back to the top).

lick_groups.title: Lick 2 · Arpeggio up, ♭9 down
lick_groups.note: climb the ii chord 1-3-5-7, then come down the V chord through its ♭9, the spicy note that pulls into the next chord. Use it in bars 4 and 12.

lick_groups.title: Lick 3 · The long turnaround
lick_groups.note: two bars, one chord each: climb the ii chord in bar 9 and hold the top, then run down the V chord in bar 10 and land on the 3rd of the I chord in bar 11.

licks_practice: sing the lick before you play it, so your ear knows where it is going.
finger it silently, then play it slowly with long-short eighth notes.
the last note is the 3rd of the next chord. Hold it with a full sound.
play the blues with arpeggios and put the lick in its bar every chorus.
change one or two notes, or the rhythm, and it becomes your own lick.
lick_chorus_note: Two choruses with everything put together. Each chorus has short licks in bars 4 and 12 and the long turnaround lick in bars 9-10 (orange); the other bars swap between arpeggios, scales and patterns. Each bar is labelled.
practice_tip: play Section 1 until the chord tones are automatic, then Section 3. Learn one lick at a time, play the Lick Chorus slowly, then write your own line here, aiming for a chord tone on beats 1 and 3.
